To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the degradation of 8 different pesticides was evaluated in soils pretreated with the respective hydrolysis products of these compounds, and that the presence of the hydrolysis metabolite in the soil conditioned the soil to enhance degradation of the parent compound.

the presence of pesticide hydrolysis products can influence the rate of degradation for some soil‐applies pesticides, and that this phenomenon is a potential mechanism for the induction or inhibition in enhanced pesticide degradation.
the degradation of 2‐4‐D, parathion and isofenfos was enhanced when their respective hydrolytic products were added to the soil.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of pesticides and their degradation products on the degradation of other pesticides.
the degradation of pesticides in soil, and the effect of soil on the persistence of pesticides.
the effects of pesticide degradation products on the fate of pesticides in the soil environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of hydrolysates of pesticides in soil can influence the persistence of their parent compounds, either enhancing or inhibiting their degradation.
the presence of hydrolysates in soil may enhance the degradation of the parent pesticide.
the presence of hydrolysates of the pesticides studied had no effect on degradation of the parent compound.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of a pesticide hydrolysis product can induce enhanced degradation in soil of its parent pesticide.
pesticide hydrolytic metabolites are not always responsible for the induction of enhanced degradation in soil, but they can influence the rate of degradation when they are present in the soil.
pesticide degradation is influenced not only by the chemical structure of the parent compound but also by its hydrolysis products.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hydrolysis metabolite of a pesticide may not necessarily be a degradation intermediate in the microbial degradation of its parent compound in soil.

pesticide metabolites can be a major factor in determining the fate of the pesticide in the soil environment and that their presence can have significant implications for pesticide persistence in the environment and for the efficacy of microbial pesticide biodegradation.
the hydrolysis of pesticides is an important step in the overall degradation of the parent compound in soil.
